## Introduction {#sec-intro}

Consumers are good at indicating which product they like best. They are often less certain about whether they would buy it. Choice-based conjoint analysis, the workhorse of stated-preference measurement in marketing [@Allenby_2019], has a device for separating the two: the dual-response format [@Brazell_2006]. In each task, the consumer first makes a forced choice among the displayed product profiles and then answers a follow-up question about whether she would purchase her selection. The format was introduced to fix a practical problem with the traditional no-choice option: tasks in which "none of these" is chosen carry no information about attribute preferences. The dual-response format recovers that lost information without systematically biasing the preference estimates [@Brazell_2006; @Dhar_2003]: the forced choice always reveals preference among profiles, while the follow-up still measures demand for the category. Following its implementation in Sawtooth Software's widely used choice-based conjoint (CBC) system [@Diener_2006; @Sawtooth_2017], the dual-response format became common practice in commercial conjoint research. The format was not, however, derived from a behavioral model of the consumer. This paper supplies such a model for an ordinal follow-up. It rationalizes the dual-response format, determines the link function, and extends the purchase question from binary to ordinal.

A consumer facing a dual-response conjoint task can indicate her most-preferred product profile in the forced choice, but whether she would purchase her selection concerns a hypothetical future occasion about which she remains uncertain. That second question has traditionally been binary: "would you buy the option you selected above?", answered yes or no and modeled by pairing a multinomial logit for the forced choice with a binary logit for the purchase question [@Diener_2006; @Hung_2025_dual]. A yes-or-no answer asks her to settle something she has not yet had reason to settle, when what she holds is a probability [@Manski_1990]; a finer scale would ask for the probability itself and carry more information about what she will do. In an ordinal dual-response follow-up the question becomes "how likely are you to buy the option you selected above?", answered on a five-, seven-, or eleven-point scale from "very unlikely" to "very likely." The case for asking this way is not new. @Juster_1966 replaced the yes/no buying-intentions question with an eleven-point probability scale, @Morrison_1979 showed that stated intentions predict purchases only probabilistically and that the mapping between them depends on context, and @Manski_2004 argues for eliciting it rather than forcing a round to zero or one.

We formalize that uncertainty as a component of utility for the outside good that the consumer has not resolved at the moment she answers. That premise makes the two responses separable, which keeps the model as tractable as the standard choice model, and it determines the form of the second response rather than leaving it to be assumed. The existing binary models are the case in which she resolves the uncertainty before answering, so what they assume about her becomes explicit and testable.

To our knowledge, no prior work derives the forced choice and the ordinal purchase answer from a single account of the consumer. We make four contributions. First, we develop the behavioral model: a model of dual-response conjoint in which the consumer's unresolved uncertainty about the outside good is the only new assumption, together with the likelihood it implies and the conditions under which its parameters are identified. Second, we analyze the information content of the ordinal follow-up: we derive the information a scale with a given number of points contributes and show that it is always non-negative and never falls when the scale is made finer, extending the binary efficiency results of @Brazell_2006 and @Hung_2025_dual and providing design guidance on how many scale points to use. Third, we provide estimation routines: maximum likelihood for the aggregate model and a custom Markov chain Monte Carlo sampler for the hierarchical Bayesian model with heterogeneous preferences, including an extension with consumer-specific cut points that accommodates individual differences in scale usage [@Greene_2010; @Falco_2015]. We also express the model in Apollo [@Hess_2019] both as a check on our implementation and as a route for readers already working in that framework. Fourth, we supply evidence: simulation studies that demonstrate parameter recovery and quantify the losses from dichotomization and constant-probability weighting, and an empirical application to a commercial choice-based conjoint study with an ordinal dual response, conducted in partnership with a consumer insights consultancy. Complete replication code accompanies the paper, with each study in the simulation program laid out as an executable notebook.[^replication]

We contribute to several literatures. Marketing work on dual-response and no-choice designs set the conventions for estimating such models [@Brazell_2006; @Diener_2006; @Haaijer_2001; @Hung_2025_dual], and the format itself is still being refined. @Schlereth_2017 separate the forced and the free questions into blocks and add an adaptive rule for choosing which free questions to ask, which limits context effects and extreme response behavior when willingness to pay is the target; our likelihood presumes the two questions are asked together, so designs that separate them fall outside it (@sec-discussion). @Hung_2025_nochoice show that the appeal of the no-buy option shifts as a consumer works through the choice tasks, a drift our cut points absorb and our task-order diagnostic detects. The opt-out literature in choice modeling documents the consequences of getting the no-buy option wrong: misspecifying it degrades the accuracy of both willingness-to-pay estimates and market-share forecasts [@Campbell_2019]. Our model replaces that constant with cut points estimated from the data.

The separation of the two decisions is older than the dual-response design. Demand models fit to supermarket scanner data have long estimated whether a household buys in a category separately from which brand it picks, joining the two stages through the inclusive value of the brand-choice stage [@Gupta_1988; @Bucklin_1992]. We put that device on survey data, where the second stage reports a stated probability rather than a revealed purchase.

Our statistical tools come from work on ordered and mixed response formats, from frameworks that handle ratings, rankings, and choices together [@Marshall_2002] to ordered-choice models that let different people use the same scale differently [@Greene_2010; @Falco_2015]. Closest to our likelihood is the choice-ordered logit of @Webb_2021, which pairs a multinomial logit with an ordered logit for a rating of the chosen alternative. Their ordinal response grades that alternative's own utility; ours reports a purchase probability measured against an outside good the consumer has not resolved, which is what puts the no-buy margin into the second response. A parallel literature in transport and environmental valuation asks respondents how certain they are of each choice and models that answer jointly with the choice itself [@Hensher_2012; @Rose_2015], with @Hensher_2012 letting the thresholds vary across respondents as our extension in @sec-hetcut does. Those designs grade confidence in the choice just made; ours grades the purchase decision that the choice sets up.

@sec-model develops the model and its likelihood, nesting, identification, information, and estimation results; @sec-simstudy reports the simulation study, @sec-analysis the empirical application, and @sec-discussion the implications for practice, including scale design; @sec-conclusion concludes, and six appendices collect the proofs, the sampler and marginal-likelihood details, the extension to correlated alternatives, the implementation in Apollo, and a worked example of the model at its smallest.

[^replication]: The repository is at <https://github.com/dyavorsky/ordinalDualresponse_paper>, and the rendered notebooks are published at <https://dyavorsky.github.io/ordinalDualresponse_paper/>.
